sections.h2: What should a Kansas home seller know about the state before reading a local guide?
sections.html:
Kansas has 105 counties, and nearly every rule that touches a house sale is run at the county level even when the law is statewide. The Kansas Department of Health and Environment, citing the 2020 Census, gives the state a population of 2,937,880, and the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 2,977,220.

Counties differ a great deal in size. Johnson County alone is estimated at 636,906 residents, and each of the state's 105 counties runs its own appraiser's office and has its own district court location. A seller in Johnson County and a seller in a smaller county face the same statutes, but they deal with different offices and different local programs.

This guide hub explains how the state is organized so you can pick the right local page. Each city and county guide on this site applies the same state rules to a specific place.

sections.h2: Which Kansas counties are the largest?
sections.html:
Johnson County is the most populous county in Kansas, and the Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate puts it at 636,906.

The Census Bureau lists Johnson County at 609,863 in the 2020 census and 268,845 housing units in 2025. Its seat is Olathe, and Overland Park is its largest city, according to the county's reference entry. The county sits on the state's eastern border with Missouri, inside the Kansas City metropolitan area.

The figures above come from Census Bureau QuickFacts and the Kansas courts district list.

sections.h2: How are Kansas courts organized for probate, foreclosure and eviction?
sections.html:
Kansas has 31 judicial districts, and the district court in the county where the property sits hears probate, foreclosure and eviction cases. Some districts cover one county, such as Sedgwick (18th), Shawnee (3rd) and Johnson (10th). Others cover several. The 31st district, for example, serves Allen, Neosho, Wilson and Woodson counties.

That structure matters for sellers in two ways. First, the clerk of the district court for your county is the contact for filing and forms. Second, local programs differ. The Kansas courts list eviction resolution or mediation programs in Douglas, Johnson and Sedgwick counties, and none are listed for most other counties.

For foreclosure, the court system points to Kansas Legal Services and the Kansas Attorney General for homeowner information, and to the Kansas Housing Resource Corporation and HUD-approved housing counselors for payment trouble. The Judicial Council has foreclosure filing forms but no standard form for a homeowner's response.

sections.h2: How does property tax work across Kansas?
sections.html:
Kansas property tax is valued by a county appraiser and billed by the county, with oversight from the Property Valuation Division of the Department of Revenue. Each county's appraiser is appointed by the board of county commissioners to a four-year term and must have at least three years of mass appraisal experience.

The yearly calendar is fixed by statute:

  • Real property is valued as of January 1 each year at fair market value, with exceptions such as agricultural land.
  • The appraiser reinspects each parcel every six years and reviews the record annually.
  • Owners can appeal to the county appraiser within 30 days after the valuation notice is mailed.
  • A taxpayer who misses that deadline can still pay under protest, first half or second half but not both.
  • Bills are paid in two installments, due December 20 and May 10 for the 2025 tax year.

The Division's 2024 ratio study showed a statewide residential median ratio of 86.8, with 46 counties at 90 or higher and 59 below 90. Sellers sometimes read that as a reason their valuation looks low, but the figure describes appraisals as a group and says nothing about a single house.

One school-finance rule applies everywhere: the first $75,000 of appraised value of residential property is exempt from the 20 mill statewide school levy for tax year 2024 and after.

sections.h2: What paperwork follows a house sale in Kansas?
sections.html:
A Kansas deed is recorded with the county register of deeds, and most sales also generate a sales validation questionnaire for the county appraiser. The questionnaire asks about the price, the date of the deed, how the sale was financed, whether the house was on the open market and whether the sale was distressed or non-arm's length.

Cash sales are covered. The form lists all cash as a financing method and offers check boxes for short sales, transfers in lieu of foreclosure, family sales and sales by a court-ordered fiduciary. The form states that anyone who falsifies the value of real estate transferred is guilty of a misdemeanor, with a fine of up to $500.

Some transfers need no questionnaire, and the exemption must be stated on the document being filed. Examples include:

  • gifts stated in the deed,
  • transfers to or from a trust without consideration,
  • divorce settlements,
  • sheriff's deeds,
  • transfers made by an executor or administrator under judicial order.

The Legislative Research Department reports that Kansas repealed its mortgage registration tax in 2019. The tax had been 0.26 percent of the debt secured by a mortgage before being stepped down from 2015 through 2018. Recording fees remain, set by statute.

sections.h2: What statewide rules come up most often for sellers?
sections.html:
A handful of Kansas rules show up in almost every distressed or inherited sale, whatever the county.

  • A homestead of up to one acre inside a city, or 160 acres of farm land, is protected from forced sale, but not from tax sales or purchase-money debts.
  • A typical eviction court case can run up to 42 days after the petition is filed, on top of the notice period.
  • A landlord who sells to a bona fide purchaser still owes the tenant any security deposit the tenant is entitled to.
  • Kansas defines fair market value as what a well-informed buyer is justified in paying and a well-informed seller is justified in accepting, in an open and competitive market, with neither party under undue compulsion.

That last definition is the one county appraisers use for tax valuation. A quick as-is sale can still close below a county valuation without anyone making a mistake, because the appraisal assumes a market with no time pressure.

Each of these topics has its own guide with the statute citations. Use them as a starting point and confirm anything that affects a closing with the county office or a Kansas attorney.

sections.h2: Which Kansas guide should you read first?
sections.html:
Start with the topic that matches your situation, then move to the place. The statewide guides on this page's list cover the rules that apply in every county, and the local guides cover how those rules play out in a specific city or county.

  • Inherited house: read the probate and estate guides first, then the county guide for the county where the house sits.
  • Behind on payments: read the foreclosure material and the homestead exemption guide, since the exemption does not stop a mortgage lender.
  • House with a tenant: read the eviction and landlord-tenant guides, which explain notices, court timing and deposits.
  • Tax bill questions: read the county property tax guide for the county that bills your parcel.

The guides are general information. Confirm details with the county office or a Kansas attorney before acting.

faqs.q: How many counties does Kansas have?
faqs.a: Kansas has 105 counties, and the Property Valuation Division's appraisal system runs in all 105. Each county has its own appraiser, clerk, treasurer and register of deeds.

faqs.q: Does Kansas still charge a mortgage registration tax?
faqs.a: No. The Kansas Legislative Research Department reports that the mortgage registration tax was repealed in 2019. Register of deeds recording fees still apply.

faqs.q: When are Kansas property taxes due?
faqs.a: For the 2025 tax year, the first installment was due December 20, 2025 and the second May 10, 2026, according to the Department of Revenue's homestead booklet. Check your county treasurer for the current dates.

faqs.q: How long do I have to appeal my Kansas property valuation?
faqs.a: Thirty days after the county appraiser mails the valuation notice. A taxpayer who misses the deadline can still pay under protest.

faqs.q: Which court handles evictions and probate in Kansas?
faqs.a: The district court in the county where the property is located. Kansas has 31 judicial districts covering all 105 counties.
